title: Oasis Brothers' First Joint Interview in 25 Years Captured in New Tour Documentary
summary: For years, the mere idea of Liam and Noel Gallagher sharing a couch — let alone a microphone — seemed about as likely as a snowball surviving a British summer. The Oasis brothers, whose combustible relationship is as legendary as their anthems, hadn't given a joint interview in over a quarter century. That drought ends with a new, still-untitled documentary capturing their 2025 reunion tour, set for an IMAX release on September 11 before landing on Disney+ internationally (and Hulu in the U.S.). Directed by Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace — the duo behind music docs "Shut Up and Play the Hits" — and produced by "Peaky Blinders" creator Steven Knight, the film promises an intimate look at the Britpop icons' massive comeback. It weaves rehearsal, backstage, and onstage footage with that long-awaited sit-down conversation. Knight, in a statement, said he "cannot wait for the world to see this film," which he believes "captures the spirit and emotion of a global cultural moment and does justice to the wit and genius of two exceptional people." He emphasized the fan story, too: lives touched and sometimes changed forever by the music. The Gallaghers' solo interviews have long been reliably riotous — Noel once called The 1975's Matty Healy a "slack-jawed fuckwit," while Liam sparred memorably with British schoolkids. But seeing them together again, especially after completing the 2025 tour without imploding, feels almost miraculous. Eric Schrier, President of Direct-to-Consumer International Originals at Disney, called the film "an intimate story of reconciliation, the power of music, and Oasis, one of the most successful and influential acts of all time." With Oscar-winning sound mixers and a top cinematographer on board, the documentary aims to be as technically impressive as it is emotionally resonant. For fans who've waited decades, September can't come soon enough.
why_it_matters: For young teens, Oasis's story shows that even the fiercest personal conflicts can be overcome, and that music can bridge divides – reunion tours can heal old wounds and inspire fans across generations.

background_read: Oasis, formed in Manchester in 1991, became one of the biggest bands of the 1990s Britpop movement (a wave of British guitar music that also included Blur and Pulp).
Their 1995 album '(What's the Story) Morning Glory?' sold over 22 million copies worldwide, with anthems like 'Wonderwall' still played everywhere.
The Gallagher brothers' public feuds were as famous as their music, leading to Oasis's breakup in 2009 after a backstage fight in Paris.
Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace directed the documentary 'Shut Up and Play the Hits' (2011) about LCD Soundsystem's final concert, and Steven Knight created the TV series 'Peaky Blinders'.
The film's IMAX release gives it a big-screen scale, while Disney+ and Hulu will bring it to millions of homes worldwide.

perspectives.description: The documentary celebrates reconciliation and shows that two brothers who once couldn't share a room can now create something monumental together again. It gives hope that broken relationships can be mended, and the 2025 tour proved they could cooperate professionally.

Some may see the film and the reunion as a money-making venture riding on nostalgia. Past feuds were so intense that a documentary might gloss over real tensions, and fans worry the truce could be fragile — another explosive fight might be just around the corner.

The film is a cultural time capsule, documenting not just a band's return but how the Britpop era's rebellious energy is remembered. It will be studied for how it shapes the legacy of 1990s guitar music and the public's appetite for reunion stories in the streaming age.

If the documentary succeeds commercially and critically, it could open the door for more legacy acts to reunite and tell their stories on screen. It might also influence how music documentaries are made, blending IMAX spectacle with deep personal interviews.
